newsitem.title: USA: New Jersey builder settles insider trading charges.
newsitem.headline: New Jersey builder settles insider trading charges.

text.p: A New Jersey builder agreed to pay $43,140 to settle civil charges that he violated securities laws by trading on confidential information about AT&T takeover targets, regulators said on Wednesday.

Without admitting or denying the allegations, Alfred Volpe agreed to pay $17,255 in ill-gotten profits plus prejudgment interest of $8,630 and a civil penalty of $17,255, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission said.
U.S. District Court Judge John Sprizzo of New York City entered the final judgment on March 5 against Volpe, who is in the construction business in New Jersey, the agency said.

In a complaint filed on October 31, 1995, the SEC alleged Volpe used insider information to buy and later sell the stocks of two companies the AT&T sought to acquire in 1991 -- Digital Microwave Corp. and Teradata Corp.
Volpe also passed his information on to another investor, James Galante, it said.

Volpe also was tipped off in early April 1991 that AT&T dropped its plans to acquire Digital Microwave and sold his shares at a profit, the agency said. He also profited on the sale of his shares of Teradata, which was acquired by AT&T's former NCR Corp. unit, it said.

Joseph Cusimano, who provided the information to Volpe, was already fined and sentenced for trading on information provided by his friend Charles Brumfield, a former AT&T labor relations vice-president, the SEC said. Brumfield also was fined and sentenced, it said.

The scheme, which extended from December 1988 to about 1993, is believed to have netted all the participants about $2.6 million in illegal profits involving four targets: NCR Corp., Paradyne Corp., Digital and Teradata. None of the companies are presently owned by AT&T.
Of 17 persons charged in the insider trading scheme, Volpe is the ninth to settle, the commission said. Litigation is pending against the eight other defendants, including Galante.
